content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors propose a new method TS-DC for unsupervised time series representation learning. In the TS-DC method, original multivariate time series is decomposed into trend and seasonality components iteratively. Then three losses L_decomp (based on decomposition error), L_{KL} (quantifies distance between distributions of the trend and seasonality components), and L_ac (use contrastive positive/negative pairs to extract complex signals in original data at different decomposition level) are designed and used to get the optimal representations. Experimental results look promising.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 9QzX: Part 1
content.comment:
> Unexplained gap between presented result and those found in the literature

> " ... I do not understand the differences between the proposed results and those that I found in the cited references. The extent of the discrepancies leads me to reject this article. "

* Many thanks for your constructive comments. In this work, we employ the same encoder as well as the same downstream model to fairly compare the effectiveness of different TS representation learners. 
* In the TS classification experiments, a Transformer-like encoder is adopted as the backbone encoder, and the downstream classifier is an RNN-based model. 
	* Most of the UCR and UEA datasets are relatively small, and the expressiveness of the Encoder and classifier adopted in our experiments cannot be fully leveraged. Therefore, the classification performance in our experiments is not as good as in other works. 
                
        * However, this is not the focus of unsupervised TS representation learning (UTSRL) models. 
        * In the experiments of this work, all UTSRL models and a supervised model are evaluated with the same backbone encoder as well as the same downstream model, such that the effectiveness of UTSRL models can be fairly compared. 
       
* We re-organize and rephrase the related implementation details in Section 4.1 and Appendix A.1 & A.2 in the revised paper accordingly. 

* Moreover, to prove that our proposed UTSRL model can achieve the classification performance reported in other related works, we conduct extra experiments on UCR and UEA datasets with different backbone encoders and downstream classifiers. 
The results are as follows: 


The averaged scores on 128 UCR datasets:


| Encoder | RNN-based | Conv-based | Transformer-based |
|:----------------:|:------------------------------:|:----------------------:|:------------------------------:|
| | ACC   AUPRC | ACC   AUPRC | ACC   AUPRC |
| LSTM | 0.302   0.284 | 0.343   0.403 | 0.454   0.686 |
| SVM | 0.536   0.321 | 0.758   0.766 | 0.643   0.332 |
| KNN | 0.481   0.308 | 0.721   0.350 | 0.596   0.325 |


The averaged classification scores on 30 UEA datasets:


| Encoder | RNN-based | Conv-based | Transformer-based |
|:----------------:|:------------------------------:|:----------------------:|:------------------------------:|
| | ACC   AUPRC | ACC   AUPRC | ACC   AUPRC | 
| LSTM | 0.250   0.235 | 0.395   0.472 | 0.399   0.569 |
| SVM | 0.608   0.216 | 0.661   0.227 | 0.623   0.235 |
| KNN | 0.540   0.230 | 0.629   0.226 | 0.590   0.215 |


> We wonder what is the hypothesis behind the decoposition of the residue: if the trend is a high energy + low frequency signal, it should be explicated at the first step.

* The hypothesis behind the decomposition is that the information will decay as the decomposition proceeds. The decomposed components in earlier steps contain more informative signals. Then, as the number of decomposition steps grows, the latter components will involve more noise.

* We plot the decomposed trend and seasonality at each decomposition level in the revised paper (please refer to Appendix C.2.2). 

    * As shown in Figure 10 in Appendix C.2.2, two datasets ECG5000 and Coffee show different characteristics: ECG5000 is of high energy and low frequency, while Coffee is of low energy and high frequency. 

    * For both two datasets, the trend and seasonality can be explicated at the first decomposition step quite well.

* Moreover, since the information contained in the remainder keeps being lowered as the decomposition proceeds, the trend and seasonality in following decomposition steps become noisier. We additionally plot the original TS as well as the recovered TS in Figure 11 in Appendix C.2.2, and the recovered TS is realized by fusing the decomposed components. It can be seen that, as the number of decomposition steps climbs up, the recovered time series fit the original data better yet more noises come along. The existence of noise does negatively affect the TS decomposition. However, this is beneficial for contrastive learning, since the robustness of the TS representation learning can be enhanced.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 9QzX: Part 2
content.comment:
> Is there a link with orthogonal matrix factorization? Or Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (to keep the recursive aspect of the approach)?

* Many thanks for your insightful questions. 
* For your first question, yes, there is a link between our TS decomposition method and orthogonal matrix factorization. 
    * In particular, we extract seasonal features with a set of trigonometric functions $S$ which can be treated as a set of orthogonal functions to exploit the properties of the Fourier Transform.
* Secondly, we address your second question below. 

The decomposition process described in our work absorbs the remainder $X^r$ recursively, such that the complex signals in the time series data can be fully captured.

Similar to traditional signal recovery algorithms, the proposed TS decomposition process works in a greedy way, like Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP), whereas, the parameters that govern the decomposition process in TS-DC are determined in an end-to-end fashion, which is different from existing signal recovery algorithms. 
    
* Besides, we have added more descriptions about the devised decomposition process in Appendix C.2.1 in the revised version, please refer to this part for more details. 
* To extract the seasonal features, we construct a set of trigonometric functions S as the set of orthogonal functions to utilize the properties of Fourier Transform


> The AUPRC metric should be described (even shortly) in the article.

* Thanks for pointing out this issue. We have described the AUPRC metric in Experiment Settings in Section 4.1 accordingly.


> I don't understand the metric & results of table 1: results (ACC around 0.4 on UCR) seem very far from what I read in the literature. I don't get the difference of setting with the cited references.

* As described above, we focus on evaluating the effectiveness of the unsupervised TS representation learning (UTSRL) model. Therefore, to fairly evaluate the UTSRL models under the same setting, we implement our UTSRL model and other baselines using the same backbone encoder and the same downstream model (e.g. classification model). Please refer to the detailed settings of how to train a UTSRL model in Appendix A.1 of the revised paper. 
* Besides, the backbone encoder and downstream classifier adopted in this work are kind of simple and naive, that's why the classification performances reported in Table 1 are not as good as other works.
* In addition, we conduct more experiments on UCR and UEA datasets with different backbone encoders and downstream classifiers. Please refer to the experimental results mentioned above.


> Sec 4.2.3 is not really meaningful, it could be moved to appendix. I also notice that the proposed TSNE does not match what I saw in the literature (in Tonekaboni 2020 for instance).

* Thanks for your suggestions and comments.
* The qualitative analysis of the representations generated by different TSRL (time series representation learning) models is an important way to examine the quality of TSRL models directly.
* Because of the class imbalance of the ECG5000 dataset, the t-SNE plots reported in Section 4.2.3 are not distinguishable as expected. It is indeed difficult to choose a UCR/UEA dataset in which the TS classes are comparable, the clustering effects can be easy to tell, and the performance differences toward downstream tasks are obvious. 
* We report an extra case study of the PenDigits dataset in Appendix C.1.2 and we will choose more representative examples in our final draft. 
* Besides, for your second question, we do not propose t-SNE, t-SNE (t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding) is a non-linear, unsupervised data exploration approach, which was proposed in 2008. t-SNE is built on top of stochastic methods, therefore, the outcomes are accompanied by randomness to a certain extent. Therefore, the t-SNE plots reported in our work might not be the same as those results in the literature.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 9QzX: Part 3
content.comment:
> On the contrary, sec 4.3.1 is a bit short: we wonder what would be the performances of each decomposition level (does-it exist a noise only level that penaliez the performances? What is the impact of the trends extracted after level 1? etc...)


* Really appreciate your constructive comments, we have added in-depth discussions about TS decomposition in Appendix C.2 in the revised paper. 
* In particular, we plot the decomposed trend and seasonality at each decomposition level in Figure 10 in Appendix C.2.2 in the revised draft. As the decomposition proceeds, more noise will get involved in the decomposed components, which could negatively affect the TS decomposition.
* However, as depicted in Figure 11 in Appendix C.2.2, by combining the latter decomposed components, the recovered TS can better fit the original TS. On the other hand, the performance of TS unsupervised representation learning can be improved because of the enhanced robustness. More specifically, the distribution space will be enlarged if noisy negative samples can be contrasted properly.


> Given the contrastive criterion, I don't understand why the ablation is so harmless on univariate TS while it is so harful on multivariate.

* We really appreciate your thoughtful comments and do hope the following explanations can address your question.
* From the ablation studies of the adaptive contrasting reported in the paper, we can draw the following conclusions:
    * For the univariate case, TS decomposition is of high quality. In particular, at the first decomposition level, the trend and seasonality preserve the most informative signals, such that the decaying weights and adaptive weighing do not affect the outcome too much.
    * On the contrary, for multivariate time series data, the perplexing high-dimensional TS is difficult to decompose. Therefore, decomposed components at latter levels can still preserve informative signals to some extent, which means that the weight decaying and adjusting is more important for multivariate TS data w.r.t. TS representation learning.

content.title: Response to Reviewer BQk8: Part1
content.comment:
> "Part of these datasets have been z-normalized while the others not, so for the convenience of training andtesting,
we standardize all the datasets and the missing values are replaced with zeros."
Please describe the z-normalization procedure in detail.
I assume that the parameters of z-normalization are derived from the train data and are applied to both train and test data. However,
I have a concern that the z-normalization could be applied to train and test data as whole,
in which case the experimental framework would be rendered invalid.
Until this concern is cleared, it is impossible to consider the acceptance of the paper.

- Notably, we do not apply z-normalization to train and test data as a whole.

- To be specific,

  - The UCR archive was first introduced in 2002 and had been expanded several times [2].
    Before 2018, the UCR archive contains 85 datasets, and the time series were already z-normalized to remove offset and scaling.
    The rationale for this step was discussed in the literature [3] as well as the report of the UCR archive [2].
    In the newly released 43 datasets, the publishers provide the raw data without any normalization when possible.
    For the UCR archive, we split the train data into train set and validate set, and apply the derived mean and std. values of the train set to the validate and test sets, separately.

  - On the other hand, for the UEA archive, we normalize the multivariate time series suggested by [3] and the preprocessing procedure in [4] (https://github.com/hfawaz/dl-4-tsc/blob/master/utils/utils.py), where the normalization is conducted on the time series data one sequence by one sequence.
    That is, the normalization is at the instance level and it is unaware of train/val/test split.

  - Besides, the classification task does not seek to predict the raw un-normalized values, as stated by [2] and [3], the differences between the train set and test set do not affect z-normalized data since z-normalization accounts for offset and scale variance.

  - Moreover, for the classification task, neither information leakage nor misguided prediction would happen when normalizing each individual time series independently in the dataset.

  - For the forecasting task, we do the normalization following the setting that you mentioned, i.e., "the parameters of z-normalization are derived from the train data and are applied to both train and test data".
    In addition, to clarify the normalization settings, we rephrase the descriptions about the normalization settings in Section 4.1 accordingly.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
In this paper, the authors propose a contrastive learning approach toward time series representation learning on top of trend-seasonality decomposition called TS-DC. Experiments on two public benchmark datasets UCR and UEA show the effectiveness of their method.  

Strengths: 
1. This paper is well-written and clear, and the proposed method is very easy to understand. 
2. The idea of utilizing the trend-seasonality decomposition method in time-series representation learning sounds interesting. 
3. After the rebuttal, the experiments become more extensive, and the performance looks good.  

Weaknesses: 
1. This paper is somehow overclaimed. The authors claim that they decompose the original time-series data into trend and seasonality. However, as shown in Figure 10, it is difficult to distinguish the trend and seasonality generated by the model. It seems that the model just roughly divides the original time-series data into positive and negative data by the fully-collected layer according to the KL divergence loss.  
2. The assumptions of this paper are too strong. Generally, the time-series data could be divided into three parts, i.e., trend, seasonality, and remainder, where the trend and seasonality are time-dependent while the remainder is usually time-independent. However, this paper only considers the trend and seasonality, and totally ignored the time-independent variable. 
3. The baselines of this paper only contain the time-series representation learning-related papers, while the seasonality-trend decomposition-related papers are missing, e.g., RobustSTL, Fast RobustSTL etc. Some other methods considering the trend and seasonality, e.g., CoST and LaST, should also be discussed in the paper.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: First, the seasonality-trend decomposition-related papers are well discussed and compared in this study. Second, the results in Figure 10 and the idea in Figure 2 are not consistent -  it is difficult to distinguish the trend and seasonality generated by the model in Figure 10. Considering some other issues raised by our reviewers, I would recommend rejecting this paper.
